title: The Venerable Ananda
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Venerable Ananda, the Buddha's attendant and the memory behind the opening formula "thus have I heard," after announcements and news of a partner's breakthrough COVID-19 case. Kanho reads a long passage from the Vinaya Pitaka in which Ananda, refused three times, wins the Buddha's consent to ordain Maha Pajapati Gotami by asking whether women can realize stream entry and arhatship. Kanho then tells of the earthquake that signals the Buddha's relinquished will to live, when Ananda misses years of hints and asks too late to keep him in the world. Kanho closes with Mary Oliver's poem "The Buddha's Last Instruction" and the four bodhisattva vows.

Yes.
Thank you.
Good evening, dear friends.
It is really good to see you tonight.
I will get to the Dharma talk itself soon, but first I want to make a few announcements, most of which make me very happy.
Great gratitude to our new communications committee, which has sent out a great email newsletter.
If you did not get it, maybe you can talk to Bob Penny after, and he'll be glad to hook you up.
It looks like we will be able to resume in-person meetings in September at the Shambhala Center on Meridian Street in Bellingham.
I believe you're going to do two streams, one in person and one on Zoom, so I think it should be available both ways.
It will be really good to sit together again.
Our Jukai retreat in November will also take place there.
Rohatsu, more good news, is also probably going to happen in person at Samish Island Camp.
We don't know yet 100% whether it's going to happen and exactly what the configuration is going to be, but it looks like it's going to happen.
Also, on July 17th there's a sangha hike.
The next announcement is on the neutral front.
We had announced originally that we would restart our Zen Alive series in mid-September.
That has been moved from mid-September to October 3rd, to facilitate a smoother transition between resident speakers and guest speakers.
So put it in your calendar: October 3rd.
The last announcement is a little more personal, and it falls into the not-so-happy category.
My partner Vedge came down with COVID-19 a few days ago.
So that's in the minus column.
The plus column, fortunately, is much fuller.
He's been fully vaccinated, and he's not very sick, nowhere near going-to-the-hospital-and-intubation sick and all that.
But maybe this is more negative-column material: he's been really cautious.
We've both always been masked up when we go away, when we go to the store, and all that social distancing.
We've been really careful, and yet he got COVID-19.
A little more than a week ago he was meeting with his son in Leavenworth and went to a restaurant a couple of times, so somewhere on the way he must have caught it.
He did pretty much everything we can do to the max, except for those two dinners out and the Airbnb.
Fortunately he's on the road to recovery, which makes me happy.
On the other hand, my insomnia, which is usually pretty bad, has been even worse.
So I apologize for all my fumbles and mistakes tonight.
I was doing my best.
It wasn't really great.
The next thing is not really an announcement, but please consider it anyway.
Breakthrough COVID-19 is a thing.
Fortunately it also means that the infection itself is going to be milder or maybe asymptomatic.
People with breakthrough cases have not usually become very ill or died; it's super rare.
Still, please don't let your guard down so much.
I need all my friends.
I love you all.
So please take care of yourself.
My cautionary tale shows that it can happen to anybody.
And my apologies for the lengthy preamble before the main body of the Dharma talk.
Oh, one more thing.
Usually Tim and the practice committee set a theme for the time.
Tim is away for his sabbatical, so that did not happen this time.
We are free range.
Any subject is up for grabs.
So I wanted to bring up an old Dharma friend of mine, the Venerable Ananda.
Ananda was the primary attendant of the Buddha and one of his principal disciples.
He stood out for having an incredible memory, in an age where people were pretty much trained to transmit information orally.
He stood out even there.
Most of the texts of the Pali Canon are attributed to his recollection of the Buddha's teachings during the first Buddhist council.
He is also known as the treasurer of the Dharma for that reason.
When we read or listen to the Buddha's discourses, they always start with some translation of the phrase "thus have I heard."
That was the formula first used by Ananda during the first Buddhist council at Rajagriha.
At this gathering the Buddhist Canon, what we call the Pali Canon today, was established, and Ananda was conveying all the teachings of the Buddha to those present.
The formula is usually completed by the place where it occurred and the names and numbers of those it was given to, followed by the actual teaching.
Ananda was the first cousin of the Buddha.
Early texts do not agree much on Ananda's life before he became a disciple of the Buddha.
He became well known when he became his attendant.
Ananda performed all the duties given to him by the Buddha with great devotion and care.
He often was the intermediary between the Buddha and lay people, and he also interacted with the Sangha on behalf of the Buddha.
He gave many Dharma talks when assigned by the Buddha to do so.
He accompanied the Buddha for the rest of his life, acting as his assistant.
This level of devotion and care truly warms my heart.
However, there is another reason why I really love Ananda.
Ananda had a very important role in the establishment of the order of the bhikkhunis or bhikkhunis, the order of nuns.
He intervened with the Buddha on behalf of the Buddha's foster mother, Maha Pachapati, whose name he just chanted in service.
Originally the Buddha did not want to include nuns in his Sangha, but Ananda's intervention allowed it to happen.
I will read you a longish excerpt from the book *Life of the Buddha According to the Pali Canon*.
A little preamble to that story, too: after King Suddhodana fell sick and died, the Buddha again visited home.

*And Maha Pachapati, she went to him and she said, "Lord, it would be good if women could obtain the going forth from the house life into homelessness in the Dhamma and discipline declared by the perfect one."
And she asked three times and she was denied three times.* The Buddha left and she stayed, remaining a householder.
The Buddha himself went on to Vesali.
In the meanwhile, Maha Pachapati cut off her hair and put on the yellow robe, and with a number of Shakyam women she walked to Vesali.
Upon arrival, she went to the place where the Buddha stayed, and she stood there outside the porch.
Now I'm reading from the book.
*Her feet were swollen, her limbs covered with dust.
And she was sad and unhappy, with tears on her face and sobbing.
As she stood thus, the Venerable Ananda saw her.
He asked her, "Kotami, why are you standing outside the porch like this?"
"Lord Ananda, it is because the Blessed One does not allow the going forth for women in the Dhamma and discipline declared by the perfect one," she said.
"Then, Kotami, wait here till I ask the Blessed One about this," Ananda said.*
*The Venerable Ananda went to the Blessed One and told him what had happened.
And he said, "Lord, it would be good if women might obtain the going forth from the house life into homelessness in the Dhamma and discipline declared by the perfect one."
"Enough, Ananda.
Do not ask for the going forth from the house life into homelessness for women in the Dhamma and discipline declared by the perfect one."
Ananda asked a second and a third time and was refused.
Then he thought, "The Blessed One does not allow it.
But suppose I asked the Blessed One in another way."

Then he said, "Lord, are women capable, after going forth from the house life into homelessness in the Dhamma and discipline declared by the perfect one, of realizing the fruit of stream entry or once return or non-return or arhatship?"
"They are, Ananda."*
*Ananda continued.

"If that is so, Lord, then since Mahapachaparikotami has been exceedingly helpful to the Blessed One when, as his mother's sister, she was his nurse, his foster mother, his giver of milk, she suckled the Blessed One when his own mother died.
Since that is so, Lord, it would be good if women could obtain the going forth."
The Buddha replied, "Ananda, if Mahapachaparikotami accepts eight capital points, that will count as her full admission.
These are the eight points.

A bhikkhuni*, bhikkhuni is the word for nun in the Buddha's time, *who has been admitted even a hundred years must* pay homage, get up for, reverentially salute *and respectfully greet a bhikkhu admitted that day.*
*A bhikkhuni must not spend the rains in a place where there are no bhikkhus.

Every half month, a bhikkhuni should expect two things from the sangha of bhikkhus: the appointment of the Uposatha day of observance each half month*, that's what we call our precepts and ceremony, *and a visit for exhortation.
At the end of the rains, a bhikkhuni must invite criticism of both sanghas in the three instances.
That is, whether anything improper in her conduct has been seen, heard or suspected.
When a bhikkhuni has committed a grave offense, she must do penance before both sanghas.*
*A probationer who seeks admission must do so from both sanghas and after training in the six things for two years.
A bhikkhuni must not find fault with or abuse a bhikkhuni in any manner at all.
From today onwards, it is not allowed for bhikkhunis to address discourses to bhikkhus, but it is allowed for bhikkhus to address bhikkhunis.
These eight things are to be honored, respected, revered and venerated, and they are not to be transgressed as long as life lasts.
If Maha Pachapati Gotami accepts these eight capital points, that will count as her full admission."
So Ananda went to Maha Pachapati Gotami and told her what the Blessed One had said, and Maha Pachapati accepted.
She said, "I accept these capital points, not to be transgressed as long as life lasts."*
*Ananda went back to the Buddha and told him about Maha Pachapati's response.

And the Buddha said, "Ananda, if women had not obtained the going forth from the house life into homelessness, in the Dhamma and discipline declared by the Perfect One, the holy life would have lasted long, the holy life would have lasted a thousand years.
But now, since women have obtained it, the holy life will not last long, the holy life will only last 500 years."*
When we usually talk about the Pali Canon, our talks are based on the Sutta Pitaka, the basket of talks.
This story came from the Vinaya Pitaka, the basket of rules and regulations, since it regulates the place of the nuns in the Sangha of the Buddha's time.
Ananda was truly beloved by the Buddha and often praised for his eloquence, for his compassion, for his kindness.
Nevertheless, he was also often reprimanded.
The criticisms included that Ananda had worldly attachments, his failure to attain enlightenment, and taking stands opposing the Buddha, such as pleading the case of Maha Pachapati.
And yet, and yet, Ananda is a patriarch in our lineage, a patriarch of the Dhamma, and he has been beloved and honored by Buddhist women for obvious reasons.
Shortly after the Buddha's death, I'm going to jump around a little.
I'm going to do one more return.
Shortly after the Buddha's death, the first council was convened, and Ananda was told, "You can't come unless you become enlightened."
So he just threw himself totally into it.
And he made it that close.
It was really close.
But that's another story; you'll have to look it up yourself.
He had an important role during the first Buddhist council.
He was the living memory of the Buddha, reciting the stories and the teachings and checking what others said for accuracy.
But during the same council, again, he was chastised by Mahakasyapa and the rest of the Sangha for allowing women in, because everybody was so sure we would throw in everything.
And he failed to understand the Buddha at several crucial moments.
So I want to jump back to one more of the criticisms that Ananda endured, and that was that it was Ananda's fault that the Buddha died so early.
That will be our last story for tonight.
Over the years, the Buddha had dropped hints that he might live for a long, long time.
But he never said, like, "You need to specifically ask me to live for a long time."
He just said, "Oh, a Buddha can live for a very long time."
He went hint, hint, hint, and Ananda did not get the hints.
When the Buddha became enlightened, we all know the story about Mara showing up.
He told the Buddha, "You're enlightened now.
You could just like die.
You did everything.
So why not just die?"
When Mara said, "Let the Blessed One attain final nirvana now," the Buddha told him that he would not do that until he had established a very solid Sangha that would carry on after his death.
One day, when the Buddha was already old, Mara came by again.
He said, "Hey, you have your Sangha.
It's time to go."
And the Buddha agreed.
It caused a huge earthquake, and Ananda felt the earthquake.
He came to the Buddha and said, "Blessed One, there was this huge earthquake.
What does it mean?"
And the Buddha told him that he had relinquished his will to live.
When he heard this, the Venerable Ananda said:
*Lord, let the Blessed One live out the age.
Let the Sublime One live out the age for the welfare and happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, the welfare and the happiness of gods and men.*
And the Buddha replied:
*Enough, Ananda, do not ask that of the perfect one now.
The time to ask that of the perfect one has now gone by.*
The second time, the Venerable Ananda made the same request and received the same answer.
And the third time, the third time, the Blessed One said:
*Have you faith in the perfect one's enlightenment, Ananda?*
*Yes, Lord.*
*Then why do you press the perfect one up to the third time?*

*Lord, I heard and learned this from the Blessed One's lips: when anyone has maintained and* developed *the four bases of success, made them a vehicle, made them the foundation, established, consolidated and properly undertaken them, he could, if he wished, live out the age or what remains of the age.*
*Have you faith, Ananda?*
*Yes, Lord.*
And then the Buddha said:
*Then, Ananda, the wrongdoing is yours, the fault is yours.
For even when such a broad hint, such a plain sign was given by the perfect one, you could not understand it.
And you did not beg the perfect one to live out the age for the good, the welfare and happiness of gods and men.
If you had done so, the perfect one would have refused you twice, and then at the third time he would have consented.
So, Ananda, the wrongdoing is yours, the fault is yours.*
And then the Buddha goes on, in painful detail, to recount all the times where he had dropped hints to Ananda.
So he would ask him three times to live for a long time.
That is the end of the talk today, but I don't want to leave you here with such a sad story.
So I'm going to read you a poem I've read to you often before.
It's "The Buddha's Last Instruction" by Mary Oliver.
*Make of yourself a light, said the Buddha before he died.
I think of this every morning as the East begins to tear off its many clouds of darkness to send up the first signal, the white fan streaked with pink and violet, even green.
The old man, he laid down between two solid trees.
And he might have said anything, knowing that it was his final hour.
The light burns upward, it thickens and settles over the fields.*
*Around him, the villagers gathered and stretched forward to listen.
Even before the sun itself hangs, disattached in the blue air, I am touched everywhere by its ocean of yellow waves.
No doubt he thought of everything that had happened in his difficult life.
And then I feel the sun itself as it blazes over the hills, like a million flowers on fire.
Clearly I am not needed, yet I feel myself turning into something of inexplicable value.
Slowly, beneath the branches, he raised his head.
He looked into the faces of that frightened crowd.*
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place, with the true merit of Buddha's word.*
*Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*

May our intention equally extend to every being and place, with the true merit of Buddha's word.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them. Illusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them. Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them. Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.
